clips.title: Welcome aboard: leaving the capital
clips.text:
Good morning, Julia! Good morning, Adam! And a big hello to our trusty driver. I'm your guide for today, a proud NorCal local, and I am stoked to show you around. We're going from the capital to the redwoods: across a floodplain, over the hills into wine country, and down to the Russian River at Guerneville. I'll pipe up when there's something good, and I'll keep quiet when there isn't.

Okay, first quiz of the day, nice and easy. Before the levees went up, Sacramento flooded so often that the city did something kind of wild about it. What do you think they did? … They raised the streets. A whole storey! That's why there are still tunnels and buried old storefronts under Old Sacramento, the riverside district with all the nineteenth-century brick buildings, the most famous ones built right after a huge fire in 1852.

And that golden lift bridge you might have spotted? That's the Tower Bridge, opened in 1935, with towers 160 feet tall. On opening day they released a thousand homing pigeons to carry the news across California. Pigeons! It got painted gold in 2002 after a public vote, and honestly, some locals are still grumbling about it. Alright, gang. Let's head west.

clips.title: Sam Brannan, California's first millionaire
clips.text:
Okay, here's a name you're going to hear all day: Sam Brannan. Total character. He was a printer and a Mormon elder who sailed a whole shipload of Latter-day Saint emigrants around Cape Horn to California in 1846, and he packed a printing press and an entire flour mill for the trip. He started the California Star, San Francisco's first newspaper, and he's considered the first guy to spread the word about the Gold Rush. Then his stores supplied the rush, and boom: California's first millionaire.

He bought land everywhere, including a hot-springs valley at the top of Napa Valley that he named Calistoga. Hang on to that one. There's a great story coming.

Sadly, it didn't end well for Sam. He helped form San Francisco's first vigilance committee, which got him kicked out of his church. His wife divorced him, and he had to sell off a lot of his land to pay her half. He died poor and pretty much forgotten. His house in Old Sacramento, built in 1853, is still standing, though.

clips.title: West Sacramento: the Town of Washington
clips.text:
Alright, first town of the day, and what a way to start. Picture it: 1849. A guy named James McDowell starts a bar fight, and loses it fatally. He leaves behind his wife Margaret, three daughters and 600 acres. And Margaret? She doesn't fall apart. She hires a surveyor, carves the land into forty-one blocks, and sells lots in a brand-new town she names the Town of Washington. Total boss move.

That's where you are now: West Sacramento, in Yolo County. Washington became a rest stop for exhausted travellers slogging through the marshes to Sacramento, and a busy fishing town, shipping salmon, sturgeon and crayfish all the way to San Francisco. Later it got renamed Broderick, and in 1987 it finally merged with its neighbours to become one city.

Quick one: West Sacramento is over a hundred miles from the ocean, by river. But it has a port for ocean-going ships. How do the ships get here? … A 43-mile deep-water channel, dredged all the way up from Suisun Bay, opened in 1963. Mostly they ship out rice.

clips.title: The Yolo Bypass: a floodplain on purpose
clips.text:
Okay, look out the windows, both sides. All that flat land? This is one of the cleverest bits of flood control in America, and you're driving right over it on the Yolo Causeway, a three-mile-long bridge.

Here's the trick. Instead of building taller and taller walls around Sacramento, engineers just gave the river somewhere else to go. Upstream there's a concrete spillway called the Fremont Weir. When the Sacramento River gets too high, the extra water simply pours over the top, into this basin. In a big flood this whole area becomes a shallow inland sea, about forty miles long and three miles wide, carrying several times the flow of the river itself. And the causeway keeps you high and dry above it all.

Why bother? Because the floods of 1862 and 1878 absolutely drowned this valley. Congress signed off on the plan in 1911, and the Army Corps of Engineers laid out the bypass in the early thirties.

In the dry months it's mostly farmland. And in winter they flood the rice fields after harvest, so thousands of ducks and shorebirds hang out in plain view of the freeway. So if you see water and birds out there, don't worry. That's the plan working.

clips.title: The causeway, the Tule Jake Road, and a quarter of a million bats
clips.text:
Want to know who lives under this bridge? Have a guess. … Bats! Roughly a quarter of a million Mexican free-tailed bats migrate to the Yolo Causeway every June. They squeeze into the expansion joints between the concrete sections and feast on bugs from the wetlands. It's one of the biggest bat colonies in California, and there are actual bat-watching tours at dusk.

Before any causeway existed, crossing this basin in the wet season meant a ferry, or a long detour south through Stockton. In summer, the first vehicle to make it across set the route of the Tule Jake Road. The first causeway opened in 1916 and they threw a three-day party for it. In 1928 it became part of the Lincoln Highway, the first road across America. Today's twin bridges date from 1962, and the traffic reporters call them the long bridge and the short bridge.

clips.title: Davis: the university farm
clips.text:
Coming up is Davis, and here's a quiz for you, Adam and Julia. Davis is famous for one particular way of getting around. Any guesses? … Bikes! It's so flat that it calls itself the bicycling capital of America, and it's even home to the United States Bicycling Hall of Fame.

Davis started out as a railroad stop in 1868, named Davisville after a local farmer, Jerome C. Davis. Then in 1907 the post office got tired of all those extra syllables and just chopped it down to Davis. Classic.

The big deal here is the university. Back in 1905 the state picked Davis from about fifty sites for a university farm, partly because Berkeley's own agriculture dean admitted that foggy Berkeley was terrible for farming. The farm opened in 1908 and grew into UC Davis, and its vet school is the biggest in the country.

And two very Davis oddities. In 1972, students built a little village of fibreglass geodesic domes, inspired by Buckminster Fuller, and people still live in them today. And Muir Commons, finished in 1991, is known as the first newly built cohousing community in the United States. Very Davis.

clips.title: UC Davis and the wine revolution
clips.text:
Okay, wine nerds, this one's for you. UC Davis keeps popping up in the wine story all day. Back in 1903 the federal government set up an experimental vineyard at Oakville, in the Napa Valley, and UC Davis still runs it. In 1935, the Wolfskill family, the farming pioneers of Winters, gave the university a hundred acres of their old ranch for an experimental orchard.

Quiz: in 1951, UC Davis produced its very first graduates in the science of growing grapes and making wine. How many were there? … Just seven! And one of them, Joe Heitz, went on to make one of Napa's most famous Cabernets, Martha's Vineyard, which was one of the California reds at the legendary 1976 Paris tasting. And since 2008, the campus has had a wine and food institute named after Robert Mondavi, the guy who did more than anyone to put Napa on the map. You'll hear about him soon.

clips.title: The Patwin: the people of this valley
clips.text:
Let's rewind way, way back. Long before the farms, the freeway and the bikes, this edge of the Sacramento Valley belonged to the Patwin, the southern branch of the Wintun peoples, who've lived around here since roughly the year 500.

They lived in settled villages, fishing, hunting and gathering, and the big one was acorns. All those oak groves on the plains and foothills? That was the harvest. Here's something cool: their group names are still all over today's map. The Ululatos lived where Vacaville is now, around a village on Ulatis Creek. The Labaytos lived along Putah Creek, the Malacas in Lagoon Valley, the Tolenas up the Suisun Valley, and the Suisunes on the Suisun Marsh, which is named after them. One of the most famous Patwin leaders was Sem-Yeto, better known as Chief Solano, a diplomat and a friend of the Mexican general Vallejo.

Then the Gold Rush hit, and it was devastating. Settlers took the oak groves and the water. Smallpox and measles swept through. A lot of Patwin people were forced into unpaid work on ranches and in mines, which historians describe as another form of slavery. By the late 1850s the population had collapsed, and by the 1920s nobody was left along Putah Creek.

But here's the good part: the Patwin are still here. Today they belong to three federally recognised tribes, including the Yocha Dehe Wintun Nation, and the language, listed as at risk in 1997, is being taught to kids again. And near Fairfield, a hillside park that opened in 2024 has a Patwin name: Patwino Worrtla Kodoi Dihi, meaning Southern Rock Home of the Patwin People, run together with the Yocha Dehe.

clips.title: Dixon: the town that moved to the tracks
clips.text:
Here's a fun one. Dixon, coming up, is a town that literally picked itself up and moved.

During the Gold Rush there was a little settlement called Silveyville around here, a halfway stop for miners heading between the coast and the gold fields. Then the railroad showed up in 1868, and it missed Silveyville by a few miles. Awkward. So in 1871 the whole town just relocated, buildings and all, to sit next to the tracks. The Methodist church on North Jefferson Street made the trip.

Quiz time. The new town was supposed to be called Dicksville, after Thomas Dickson, who donated the land for the depot. So how did it end up as Dixon? … A typo! In 1872 the first train shipment from San Francisco arrived addressed to Dixon, and everybody just shrugged and went with it.

A couple more Dixon brags: the Dixon May Fair, started in 1885, is billed as California's oldest fair. A local pumpkin patch keeps breaking the Guinness record for the world's biggest corn maze, one of them sixty acres. And near where Highway 113 meets the interstate, there's a hundred-foot-tall sign for the old Milk Farm Restaurant. The sign went up in 1963, and it's still standing, way after the restaurant closed.

clips.title: Why the valley is so flat: seven miles of buried sea floor
clips.text:
Okay, geology time, and I promise this one's cool. Question: why is this valley so ridiculously flat? … Because you're driving across the top of a giant filled-in hole.

Back when dinosaurs were around, between about 150 and 65 million years ago, this whole valley was a seaway. To the east, where the Sierra Nevada is now, there was a chain of volcanoes. To the west, an ocean plate was diving under North America, and the rocks scraped off it piled up into a ridge that worked like a dam. In between was a deep basin, and the volcanoes eroded straight into it, sending mud and sand down underwater canyons. Geologists call the result the Great Valley Sequence, and in places it's around 40,000 feet thick. That's over seven miles of stacked-up sea floor.

And here's the mind-blowing bit. The volcanic top of the ancient Sierra was mostly stripped off and used to fill this valley. You're basically driving over a mountain range that got flattened and poured into a bowl.

Those old sea-floor rocks come up to the surface along the western edge of the valley, in the hills ahead of us. Right under the freeway, the geological maps show the most recent layers: sand and gravel fanned out by creeks, and low ridges called natural levees that rivers build when they flood. So this flat farmland is just the top layer of a seven-mile stack of history.

clips.title: Vacaville and the quarrel over Rancho Los Putos
clips.text:
Coming up is Vacaville, and its founding story is a little shady. Here's how it went down.

In 1841, two guys from New Mexico, Juan Manuel Vaca and Juan Felipe Peña, came to California, and in 1843 they were granted a huge ranch called Rancho Los Putos: over 44,000 acres, stretching almost all the way to Davis. Peña's adobe house, built in 1842, is still standing, the oldest building around here.

Then in 1850, Vaca sold some land to a man named William McDaniel, on the condition that a square mile would become a town called Vacaville. McDaniel's business partner, a lawyer, acted as interpreter, because Vaca couldn't read or write English. Quiz: Vaca thought he was signing away one square mile. How much did he actually sign over? … Nine! Vaca was furious. He took out a notice in the newspaper warning everyone not to buy land from McDaniel. Peña was mad too, and it wrecked their friendship.

Vacaville grew rich on fruit, with lots of Japanese and Chinese workers in the orchards and packing houses. And a more recent claim to fame: in August 2022, a truck crashed on the freeway here and splattered over 150,000 tomatoes across the eastbound lanes. It made international news. Ketchup, anyone?

clips.title: The Nut Tree: a fruit stand that fed a Queen
clips.text:
Coming up near the junction with Interstate 505 is the Nut Tree. Today it's a shopping centre, but it used to be a legit California legend.

It opened on the 3rd of July 1921 as a tiny fruit stand on the old Lincoln Highway, run by Helen and Ed Power. It's named after a black walnut tree that grew from a nut a pioneer girl, Sallie Fox, picked up on a trail in Arizona before she got here in 1859.

The stand blew up. By year two it was serving around 950 cars a day. Then it grew into a restaurant with a floor-to-ceiling glass aviary, a bakery, a toy shop, and its own little train out to its own airport. Charles Eames designed the furniture! It's even credited as an early pioneer of California cuisine, all fresh fruit and veg.

Quiz! Reagan, Nixon and Bing Crosby all stopped by the Nut Tree. But in 1983 it catered lunch for someone even fancier. Who? … Queen Elizabeth the Second! Not bad for a fruit stand. The original closed in 1996.

clips.title: The Vaca Mountains: the first wall of the Coast Ranges
clips.text:
See that ridge rising up to the west? Those are the Vaca Mountains, the very first wall of California's Coast Ranges, and the thing standing between this flat valley and all the wine country we're about to see.

Quiz: once we cross over those hills, everything gets a lot greener. Why do you think that is? … Rain shadow! The Vacas are the furthest range from the ocean, so the clouds have already dropped most of their rain on the mountains further west. That's why the ridgetops here are dry chaparral: chamise, manzanita and buckbrush.

The east face of the Vacas shoots straight up, a thousand feet or more above the foothills. The highest point, Mount Vaca, is 2,818 feet, the top of Solano County, and the long, flat backbone is called the Blue Ridge.

Since almost all the rain falls in winter, by late summer and fall these hills are tinder-dry. In August 2020, the Hennessey Fire burned through here and destroyed farms and homes in Vacaville. We'll hear more about those fires later.

clips.title: Travis Air Force Base: the Gateway to the Pacific
clips.text:
Eyes on the sky, team! If you spot something huge and grey lumbering overhead, it's almost definitely coming from Travis Air Force Base, a few miles east of Fairfield.

Travis calls itself the Gateway to the Pacific, and it moves more cargo and passengers than any other military air terminal in the United States. It flies massive C-5 Galaxies, C-17s and KC-46 tankers, and it's the biggest employer in the whole county.

It started in 1942, ferrying planes and supplies out to the Pacific in the Second World War. After the war it became a bomber base for B-29s, B-36s and later B-52s.

And the name comes from a pretty dramatic story. In August 1950, a B-29 carrying a nuclear bomb, without its nuclear core thank goodness, crashed just after take-off. The fire set off the bomb's regular explosives, killing Brigadier General Robert Travis and eighteen others. The base was named after him the following year.

clips.title: Fairfield, Cordelia, and a captain's sense of home
clips.text:
Fun fact about the next two towns: they were both named by the same guy, a clipper ship captain called Robert H. Waterman. He named Fairfield after his hometown back in Connecticut. And in 1853 he started a little settlement he called Bridgeport. When the post office asked for something more original, he renamed it after the most important person in his life. Any guesses? … His wife, Cordelia! Aww.

Waterman also pulled off a sneaky political move. In 1858 he entered Fairfield in the race to become the county seat, and won it away from Benicia, helped by offering sixteen acres of free land for county buildings. Fairfield's been the county seat ever since.

And one more local secret. In the hills here there used to be a company town called Cement, founded in 1902 to quarry limestone and make cement. clips.title: The Rockville Stone Chapel and a congregation split by war
clips.text:
Just north of Cordelia, in the Suisun Valley, there's a little stone church with a big story: the Rockville Stone Chapel, built by volunteers in 1856. The stone is volcanic ash rock from the nearby hills, and it's soft and easy to cut when it comes out of the ground, then hardens once it's exposed to air. How handy is that?

The land was donated by Landy Alford, who came west in 1846 in the same wagon train as the famous Donner Party, and his son-in-law later helped rescue the survivors.

Then the Civil War split the church. The congregation divided over slavery, and on Christmas Eve 1863, the northern supporters literally walked out. The southern-leaning members who stayed put up a plaque reading M.D. Church South, and it's still there. The chapel fell apart for decades, got restored in 1940, and it's still in use today.

clips.title: The Suisun Marsh
clips.text:
Off to the south is a place where people tried to farm for about fifty years, and gave up because it got too salty even for the cows. That's the Suisun Marsh, described as the biggest brackish-water marsh on the whole west coast: over a hundred thousand acres of tidal marsh and sloughs, where fresh river water meets the salty bay. It's named after the Suisunes, a Patwin group who lived here.

During the Gold Rush, hunters shot ducks and geese here to sell fresh birds and feathers in San Francisco's markets. From the 1880s, farmers built levees and tried to grow crops, until the soil got too salty even for cattle. Then the big water projects upstream made it saltier still. These days it's home to river otters, native fish and pelicans.

clips.title: The railroad that beat the Golden Spike
clips.text:
Okay, here's a story with a twist. Quiz first: when the transcontinental railroad was finished with the famous golden spike in May 1869, where did it actually end? … Sacramento! Not the Pacific. Getting trains the rest of the way to San Francisco Bay was a whole separate race.

And the tracks beside this freeway? They won a part of that race. They were built by the California Pacific Railroad, to link Vallejo, on the bay, with Sacramento. The line was finished in November 1868, six months before the golden spike, so from early 1869 you could take a ferry from San Francisco to Vallejo and catch the train from there. Towns like Davis and Dixon grew up around its stations, and it even had a branch up the Napa Valley to Calistoga.

Of course the big Central Pacific wanted it. When the owners said no to their offer, Central Pacific threatened to build a rival line right next to it, bought up most of the stock, and took over. Then they built a shortcut across the Suisun Marsh, which took two years because the marsh was so squishy it needed tons of crushed rock. From 1879, entire trains crossed the Carquinez Strait on a giant ferry.

And the line's still busy. Amtrak's Capitol Corridor trains follow the old route, and the California Zephyr and the Coast Starlight roll right through Dixon without stopping.

clips.title: From the Lincoln Highway to Interstate 80
clips.text:
This road you're on has had a few identities. In 1913, the Lincoln Highway was dedicated: the dream of an Indiana entrepreneur, Carl Fisher, and one of the first highways in America built for cars, running all the way from Times Square in New York to San Francisco. In 1928, it was rerouted across the Yolo Causeway and through Davis, Dixon, Vacaville and Fairfield, pretty much where you are right now.

Then it became Highway 40, and roadside spots like the Nut Tree fruit stand grew up along it. In the fifties and sixties it was rebuilt as Interstate 80, the main coast-to-coast route from New York to San Francisco.

Quick quiz: old Highway 40 used to run through here. Where does it end now? … Utah! It got cut back that far. And the freeway's still changing: the toll express lanes between Fairfield and Vacaville only opened in December 2025.

clips.title: Jameson Canyon: through the hills on the Lincoln Highway
clips.text:

So these hills are basically old beaches and sea floor, folded up and lifted high.

And from here on, we start meeting the rock that runs the whole show today: the Sonoma Volcanics, lava flows that erupted between about eleven and three million years ago. Over that ridge? Wine country, baby.

clips.title: Entering the Napa Valley
clips.text:
Welcome to the Napa Valley, everybody! This is the big one. In 1981 it became only the second official wine region in the whole country, and now it's one of the most famous wine regions on the planet, with more than 450 wineries.

Quick lay of the land. The valley floor rises gently from sea level here near the bay up to Calistoga at the far end, at the foot of Mount Saint Helena. Mountains on both sides: the Mayacamas on your left as we head north, and the Vacas on your right. And two roads run up the valley: Highway 29 on the west, and the quieter Silverado Trail on the east.

Quiz! Where do you think the name Napa comes from? … It's Native American, and the best guess is the Patwin word napo, which means house. And back in the 1850s, people even spelled it with two p's: Nappa.

The Napa wine story has three acts. Act one: a huge boom in the 1800s. Act two: a total crash, thanks to a bug, Prohibition and the Depression. Act three: an epic comeback, ending with Napa beating the French in Paris in 1976. I'll fill you in as we go.

clips.title: The 2014 South Napa earthquake
clips.text:
Somewhere just west of here, under the vineyards and marshes between American Canyon and Napa, is the epicentre of the biggest Bay Area earthquake in a quarter of a century.

Picture it: 3:20 in the morning, the 24th of August 2014. A magnitude 6.0 quake hits, shaking for ten to twenty seconds. One person was killed, about 200 were hurt, and the damage came to somewhere between 362 million and a billion dollars. Downtown Napa took a beating, even buildings that had been earthquake-proofed: the old courthouse, the post office, churches and the library.

Quiz: the fault behind it, the West Napa Fault, is about 35 miles long. When do you think it was discovered? … Only in 1976, and by a guy drilling for groundwater from Sebastopol! And in 2023 they found out it's nine miles longer than anyone thought. Cool footnote: an experimental earthquake warning system gave seismologists a few seconds' heads-up before the big shaking arrived.

clips.title: Napa: a river town
clips.text:
Picture Napa's Main Street in the 1850s: up to a hundred saddle horses tied up on any old afternoon. Yeehaw.

The city of Napa, off to the east, started life as a river town. The Napa River is tidal here, so this was as far as boats could get. The first recorded ship came up in 1842, and by 1850 a steamer called the Dolphin was carrying passengers. Nathan Coombs laid out the town in 1847 and 1848, and in 1859 John Patchett opened the county's first commercial winery, selling wine for two dollars a gallon. Two bucks!

There's a darker side to the story, though. When the first recorded expedition came into the valley in 1823, most people here were Native Americans. In 1850, fighting with American settlers turned into war, and soldiers massacred the people they found, driving the survivors north toward Clear Lake.

And a fun one to finish. In 1880 the Napa Valley Opera House opened downtown with Gilbert and Sullivan's HMS Pinafore. Jack London read there in 1905. It closed in 1914, sat empty for decades, then reopened in 2003. Quiz: what show do you think they picked for the reopening? … HMS Pinafore, of course!

clips.title: Floods, gentrification and the goddess of plenty
clips.text:
For most of its history, Napa was the town wine tourists drove straight through. That changed after a 300-million-dollar flood project around the turn of this century widened the river and raised the bridges, and the developers moved in.

The big showpiece was Copia, a center for wine, food and the arts, mostly paid for by Robert and Margrit Mondavi and named after the Roman goddess of plenty. It opened in November 2001, with galleries, theatres, a giant kitchen garden and a restaurant called Julia's Kitchen, backed by Julia Child herself. But the crowds never came, and it closed in 2008. Julia Child's cookware went to the Smithsonian! Today the Culinary Institute of America has a campus on the site, right by the Oxbow Public Market.

And across the river is one of the oldest buildings in the valley: the adobe house Cayetano Juárez built in 1840. He was a soldier under General Vallejo, and the name of his ranch, Tulucay, comes from a Patwin village. The adobe's been used as a restaurant.

clips.title: The Wine Train and Brannan's railroad
clips.text:
Keep an eye out for the Napa Valley Wine Train, which runs from Napa to St. Helena right alongside Highway 29. And believe it or not, this train went all the way to the California Supreme Court.

The tracks are old. Sam Brannan, our Gold Rush millionaire, started the Napa Valley Railroad in 1864 to haul tourists from the Vallejo ferries up to his hot-springs resort in Calistoga. Passenger service ended in 1929. Then in the 1980s, when Southern Pacific wanted to abandon the line, local entrepreneurs bought it for 2.5 million dollars to run a fancy tourist train with lunch and wine.

A lot of locals were not into it. They said the valley already had way too many visitors, and they got the state to demand a full environmental review. Quiz: who won? … The train! In 1990 the state Supreme Court ruled four to three that no review was needed, because the line was already in use. Then they spent about twenty million dollars fixing the tracks. And the fight over how many tourists this valley can handle? Still going.

clips.title: Yountville: the trapper who planted the first vines
clips.text:
Coming up is Yountville, named after George Calvert Yount, and this guy's life was basically a Western movie.

Born in North Carolina in 1794, he fought in the War of 1812, then left his family in Missouri to become a fur trapper. He reached California in 1831, hunted sea otters off the Channel Islands, then worked as a carpenter for General Vallejo in Sonoma. Through Vallejo he got a huge land grant in 1836 and became the first permanent Euro-American settler in the Napa Valley. And in 1838, he planted the valley's very first grapevines. So, Yount: the guy who started all of this.

Here's a spooky one. Yount said that in the spring of 1847 he kept having the same dream, of pioneers struggling in deep snow. And a famous writer later claimed that Yount's dream helped bring about part of the rescue of the Donner Party. Whoa.

Quiz: the town was originally laid out in 1855 with a totally different name, and had to change it because another town had it first. What was it? … Sebastopol! We'll actually meet the real Sebastopol later. Today almost a third of Yountville's residents live at the Veterans Home of California, founded in 1884, the biggest of its kind in the country.

clips.title: The French Laundry and the bubbles from Champagne
clips.text:
Okay, foodies, this one's for you. Yountville is home to The French Laundry, one of the most famous restaurants in America. And yes, it really was a laundry. The stone building went up as a saloon in 1896. Then in 1906 a law banned alcohol near the Veterans Home, and in 1920 it became a French steam laundry.

In 1978 Sally Schmitt and her husband Don, who was the mayor at the time, turned it into a restaurant and kept the old name because locals still called it that. Sally was a pioneer of California cuisine, cooking with local, seasonal ingredients. Thomas Keller took over in 1994 and won three Michelin stars. And in 2020, it was all over the national news when Governor Gavin Newsom went to a dinner there during COVID restrictions. Oops.

Also here: Domaine Chandon, opened in 1973 by the Champagne house Moët et Chandon, the first French-owned bubbly producer in the Napa Valley.

clips.title: How the Napa Valley was built: volcanoes, faults and gravel
clips.text:
Let's talk dirt! Because in this valley, the dirt is literally the product.

Shape first. Napa is a long, skinny trough between two mountain ranges, with a whole family of faults, including the West Napa Fault, slicing through and slowly sliding the land past itself.

Then: volcanoes! Between about eleven and three million years ago, this whole area was erupting. The leftovers are called the Sonoma Volcanics, lava, ash and broken volcanic rock, and the hills on both sides are full of it. There's even a low hill east of Napa that geologists think was a volcano rising up inside an old collapsed crater. Up toward the Mayacamas there's white pumice from an eruption nearly five million years ago, and glassy lava with swirly flow bands, about 5.3 million years old.

Then the creeks took over. Over the last few hundred thousand years they washed gravel and sand down out of those volcanic hills and spread it in fans across the valley floor. In the middle of the valley, around Oakville and Rutherford, there's a gravelly rise called the Rutherford Bench, where the soil drains really well.

So here's the takeaway, Julia and Adam: next time you sip a Napa Cabernet, you're partly tasting a volcano. Cheers to that.

clips.title: Oakville: To Kalon, Mondavi and Opus One
clips.text:
Okay, coming up is Oakville, population about fifty. Tiny! But it's got a juicy family drama.

First, quiz: Oakville has one of Napa's most famous vineyards, planted in 1868 and named To Kalon. That's Greek. What do you think it means? … The beautiful! The guy who planted it, H. W. Crabb, tested over 400 grape varieties to figure out what grew best here.

Now the drama. In 1965, Robert Mondavi had a huge falling-out with his younger brother Peter over the family winery, Charles Krug. clips.title: Rutherford: a sea captain, a Godfather and the sacramental wine
clips.text:
Here's Rutherford, and its most famous estate was bought with money from The Godfather. Seriously. But let's start at the beginning.

The town's named after Thomas Rutherford, who married George Yount's granddaughter. In 1864 Yount gave the couple about a thousand acres, and they planted vines.

The big estate here is Inglenook, started in 1879 by Gustave Niebaum, a Finnish sea captain who made a fortune in the Alaska fur trade. He actually wanted to build his winery in France, but his wife hated long ocean voyages, so: Napa! Decades later, the film director Francis Ford Coppola bought the estate bit by bit, starting in 1975, with his profits from The Godfather. In 2011 he even bought back the Inglenook name, and he said the name cost him more than the whole estate.

They landed a contract to supply sacramental wine to churches across the country, and demand went through the roof. By 1933 they were making over a million gallons a year. Holy moly.

clips.title: The Wappo: the brave ones
clips.text:
Long before vineyards, this valley was Wappo country. Their homelands covered the Napa Valley, the south shore of Clear Lake, the Alexander Valley and the Russian River valley.

They lived in small, independent groups, hunting and gathering, in homes made of branches, leaves and mud. And their baskets were woven so tightly they could hold water. Acorns from the oaks were a staple, and the hot springs up at Calistoga were a place of healing.

I love the old Wappo place names. Quiz: the Wappo called the area around St. Helena Anakotanoma. What do you think it means? … Bull Snake Village! Calistoga was Nilektsonoma, Chicken Hawk Place. And Mount Saint Helena was Kanamota: Human Mountain.

The name Wappo itself probably comes from the Spanish word guapo, which can mean brave. And they earned it: they fought off military campaigns by General Vallejo until a peace treaty in 1836. Sadly, what came next was devastating. From maybe one or two thousand people around 1770, the population fell to just fifty by 1880. Their language is gone now, though someone did write down its grammar. So when you see the name Caymus on a wine label, that's the name of a Wappo group who lived here first.

clips.title: St. Helena: Beringer, Krug and the castle of wine
clips.text:
Welcome to St. Helena, the heart of old Napa wine country, and quiz time! One of the valley's first great vineyards here came out of a very modern-sounding legal document. What do you reckon? … A prenup! Charles Krug started his winery here in 1861, often called the valley's first. He married Dr. Bale's daughter, and her mum insisted on a prenuptial agreement that protected twenty acres north of town. And that's exactly where Krug planted his vines. Smart lady. Much later, the Mondavi family bought the Krug winery for 75,000 dollars.

Then there's Beringer, founded in 1876. It calls itself the oldest continuously operating winery in the Napa Valley. In 1934, right after Prohibition, it became the first California winery to offer tours and tastings. And in 1939 it invited Hollywood stars like Clark Gable and Carole Lombard, and handed out maps saying All roads lead to Beringer. Historians call that the birth of Napa wine tourism. So, basically, every tasting room you see? Blame Beringer.

On Main Street, look out for a massive stone building: Greystone Cellars, built in 1889 so small growers could store and age their wine instead of selling it cheap to dealers in San Francisco. Today it's the Culinary Institute of America.

clips.title: The happy accident of White Zinfandel
clips.text:
Here's one of the great accidents in wine history. Right on Highway 29 in St. Helena is Sutter Home. In 1948 the Trinchero brothers bought it and scraped by making cheap jug wine.

In 1972, Bob Trinchero started making a pale wine from red Zinfandel grapes. Then, in 1975, about a thousand gallons of the juice stopped fermenting before all the sugar was gone. Oops! He set it aside, tasted it two weeks later, and it was sweet, pink and, in his words, pretty good. Quiz: what famous wine had he just accidentally invented? … White Zinfandel! By 1987 it was the best-selling premium wine in America. Wine snobs might sniff at it, but loads of people had their very first glass of wine thanks to this happy accident.

clips.title: Bust: phylloxera, Prohibition and the Depression
clips.text:
Okay, the Napa crash story. By 1880, this valley was booming: hundreds of vineyards, and by 1900 more than 140 wineries. Then came three punches in a row.

Punch one was tiny. A bug called phylloxera, a louse that eats grapevine roots, killed vines all over the valley. The fix was planting vines on roots that the bug couldn't hurt.

Punch two: Prohibition, in 1920. Lots of wineries just closed. A few survived making wine for churches, and growers sold grapes to people making wine at home.

Punch three: the Great Depression.

The comeback was slow, helped by a French winemaker at Beaulieu, Beringer's tourism, and a teacher-turned-winemaker called Brother Timothy, whose smiling face sold Christian Brothers wine all over the country. Then in 1965, Robert Mondavi opened his winery, and the boom was back on.

And the twist? Quiz: what do you think happened in 1983? … The bug came back! A new outbreak hit vines planted on a rootstock called AxR1, and growers had to replant about three-quarters of the affected vineyards by the late nineties. Now they're fighting a different bug, the glassy-winged sharpshooter. In wine country, the war with bugs never ends.

clips.title: The Bale Grist Mill and the redwoods of Bothe
clips.text:
Here's a cool spot coming up: the Bale Grist Mill, with its giant 36-foot waterwheel. It's one of only two water-powered mills left west of the Mississippi. And there's evidence that the rebels of the 1846 Bear Flag Revolt met here before they marched on Sonoma!

It was built in 1846 by Dr. Edward Turner Bale, an English ship's doctor who became surgeon-in-chief of the Mexican army and married General Vallejo's niece. His land stretched all the way from Rutherford to Calistoga. Settlers came from across the valley to grind their corn and wheat here, and the old-timers swore the slow-ground meal made bread that put city bread to shame. Sadly, Bale tried his luck in the Gold Rush, caught a fever, and died in 1849.

Right next door is Bothe-Napa Valley State Park, home to the furthest-inland coast redwoods of any state park in California. Our first redwoods of the day!

clips.title: Castles, cable cars and caves
clips.text:
Okay, the road into Calistoga has some seriously over-the-top wineries.

In the 2020 fire, the farmhouse burned, but the castle was fine. Of course it was. It's a castle.

Next: Sterling Vineyards, perched on a volcanic hill 300 feet up. Quiz! How do you get up to the winery? … An aerial tramway! Like a ski lift. And the building looks like it was beamed in from the Greek island of Mykonos.

And Schramsberg, started in 1862 by a German barber called Jacob Schram, with cellars dug into the hillside. Robert Louis Stevenson visited in 1880 and tasted eighteen wines. Eighteen! Now they make sparkling wine.

clips.title: Calistoga: a slip of the tongue
clips.text:
Welcome to Calistoga, at the top of the Napa Valley! Julia, Adam, this town has my favourite origin story of the day. Quiz: how do you think it got its weird name? Have a think. … It was a slip of the tongue! Sam Brannan, our Gold Rush millionaire, visited the hot springs here in 1852, fell in love, and bought more than 2,000 acres to build a spa to rival the fancy Saratoga Springs in New York. The story goes he meant to call it the Saratoga of California, but it came out as the Calistoga of Sarafornia. True or not, the name stuck!

His resort opened in 1862, and his railroad arrived in 1868, bringing San Francisco's rich and famous to soak in the waters. The little depot he built is still standing. Long before that, this was Nilektsonoma, the Chicken Hawk Place, home to several Wappo villages around the hot springs.

And the hot water is legit. In 1920, a soda fountain owner called Giuseppe Musante was drilling for cold water and hit a hot spring instead. By 1924 he was bottling it, and Calistoga sparkling water became a national brand.

Very 2020s note: Calistoga now has a hydrogen fuel-cell and battery power plant that can keep the whole town's lights on for up to 48 hours when the power gets cut during fire danger.

clips.title: Robert Louis Stevenson's squatter honeymoon
clips.text:
Here's a romantic one. In 1880, a broke, sickly Scottish writer showed up here with his new American wife. Quiz: who was he? He wrote Treasure Island. … Robert Louis Stevenson! He'd crossed an ocean and a continent to marry Fanny Vandegrift Osbourne, and friends told him the mountain air up here would help his lungs.

They tried the fancy Hot Springs Hotel, but couldn't afford ten dollars a week. So they spent their two-month honeymoon squatting, with Fanny's twelve-year-old son, in an abandoned bunkhouse at an old silver mine called Silverado, up on Mount Saint Helena. Cloth over the windows, water hauled by hand, rattlesnakes. Romantic, right?

He wrote it all up in a book called The Silverado Squatters, where he used his very first telephone and called Napa winemaking an experiment. And a lot of his notes about this scenery ended up in the descriptions in Treasure Island. There's a state park named after him at the top of Highway 29, with a trail past where the cabin stood. On a clear day up there, you can see Mount Shasta, 192 miles away.

clips.title: The Judgment of Paris
clips.text:
Okay, this is the big one. The story that put Napa on the world map.

In the early seventies, some California wines were amazing, but nobody cared, because everybody wanted French labels. A British wine merchant in Paris, Steven Spurrier, set up a blind tasting for America's 200th birthday. On the 24th of May 1976, eleven judges, mostly French wine experts, tasted the best Chardonnays and Cabernets, French versus Californian, without knowing which was which. Spurrier assumed France would win.

Quiz! What happened? … California won both! Top white: a 1973 Chardonnay from Chateau Montelena, just north of Calistoga. Top red: a 1973 Cabernet from Stag's Leap Wine Cellars, on the Silverado Trail. Time magazine ran the story, and it became known as the Judgment of Paris. A bottle of that Montelena is now in the Smithsonian, and there's even a 2008 movie about it, Bottle Shock.

And the plot twist? People are still arguing about the maths. A 2026 analysis found mistakes in the published totals, suggesting the white wine result was actually a tie with a French wine, and that by some counting methods, a French red was the judges' favourite. But the headline was written, and Napa was famous forever.

clips.title: Wine country on fire: 2017, 2020, and the insurance crisis
clips.text:
Driving through these hills, you might spot blackened tree trunks, and brand-new houses where old ones used to be. Here's the story of the fires.

On the night of the 8th of October 2017, hot, dry winds were gusting up to seventy miles an hour, and more than a dozen wildfires broke out across Northern California. One of them started at 9:43 at night near Tubbs Lane, just north of Calistoga. The Tubbs Fire raced more than twelve miles in its first three hours, through the Mark West Springs area and right into Santa Rosa. It destroyed more than 5,600 buildings, half of them homes in Santa Rosa. At the time, it was the most destructive wildfire in California history. And here's an eerie detail: it followed exactly the same path as another fire back in 1964.

Then 2020 was brutal too. A freak lightning storm sparked hundreds of fires, and the Glass Fire started above St. Helena, destroying wineries, a three-Michelin-star restaurant, and a historic resort. Calistoga had to evacuate for the second time since 2017. All told, about sixty percent of the Napa Valley has burned since 2017.

And now it's a money story. Since about 2020, seven of California’s twelve biggest home insurers stopped renewing policies in high-risk areas. People piled into the state's insurer of last resort, from 124,000 homes in 2019 to 663,000 by March 2026. So when you see a shiny new house on a burned hillside, someone probably fought really hard to insure it.

clips.title: Mount Saint Helena and the Russian princess
clips.text:

And it's volcanic, with an explosive past. Its eruptions sent avalanches of hot ash rolling across this landscape, and one of them, as you're about to hear, turned an entire forest to stone.

Want to guess the price? … Twelve million dollars. Anyone have that on them?

clips.title: Hot ground: the Sonoma Volcanics, Clear Lake and The Geysers
clips.text:
Here's a fun fact to blow your minds: you're crossing the Mayacamas Mountains, and almost everything around you was once molten.

The rock is called the Sonoma Volcanics: obsidian, pumice, ash, and lava, several thousand feet thick. It makes up most of the mountains around the Napa and Sonoma valleys, and it erupted from several vents, on and off, mostly between three and five million years ago. It's also what a lot of the wine-country soil is made of. So: lava wine. Kind of.

And the volcano story isn't over! To the north, around Clear Lake, is a volcanic field that last erupted only about 11,000 years ago, and the U.S. Geological Survey rates its threat as high. Its heat powers a place called The Geysers, up in these mountains: the largest geothermal field in the world, with eighteen power plants running on underground steam. In 2019 it made about a fifth of California's renewable energy.

Native people built steam baths there for something like 12,000 years. In the 1850s it became a fancy resort that drew Ulysses Grant, Teddy Roosevelt and Mark Twain. Quiz: there's one big problem with the name The Geysers. What is it? … There are no geysers! The steam vents are actually fumaroles. The guy who named it in 1847 got it wrong, and nobody ever bothered to fix it.

clips.title: Mark West Springs: in the path of the Tubbs Fire
clips.text:
Okay, here's a hero story. On the night of the 8th of October 2017, the Tubbs Fire came racing down this exact valley from Calistoga, heading for Santa Rosa. And nearby is Safari West, a 400-acre wildlife preserve with giraffes, rhinos, cheetahs, around 800 animals in all.

Quiz: the owner, Peter Lang, was 76 years old. When the fire came, what do you think he did? … He stayed. All night. He fought the flames by himself for more than ten hours, with nothing but garden hoses. And not a single animal died. What a legend.

This is the Mark West Springs area, named after a Scottish-American pioneer called William Marcus West, and the creek you're following runs nearly thirty miles from the mountains to the Russian River. Down the hill, the community of Larkfield-Wikiup lost about 500 homes in that fire, and just two years later, in 2019, another fire pushed right up to its edge again. A lot of what you're seeing has been rebuilt since.

clips.title: Utopias in the hills: Altruria and Fountain Grove
clips.text:
The hills north of Santa Rosa have attracted some real dreamers. Let me tell you about two of them.

In 1875, a religious leader called Thomas Lake Harris brought his followers, the Brotherhood of the New Life, here from New York to found a colony called Fountain Grove. He named his mansion Aestivossa, which he said meant high country of divine joy, in a language only he understood. And he insisted his real palace was in interspace. As you do. Meanwhile, his practical right-hand man, Nagasawa Kanaye, ran 2,000 acres of vineyards. Today Fountaingrove is a fancy neighbourhood.

Then in 1894, about thirty Christian socialists founded a commune in these hills called Altruria, inspired by a utopian novel. They grew orchards and sold their produce in San Francisco. Then they built a hotel. Quiz: how long do you think utopia lasted after that? … Not long! The hotel sank them, and by 1896, every Altrurian settlement was abandoned. Turns out paradise is expensive.

clips.title: Fulton and the Laguna de Santa Rosa
clips.text:
Coming up: a giant natural sponge! This is the Laguna de Santa Rosa, a 22-mile wetland that drains most of the Santa Rosa plain. In heavy winter rain it spreads into a shallow lake that can soak up more than 80,000 acre-feet of floodwater.

It's the wildest place in Sonoma County, the most biologically diverse, with over 200 kinds of birds, bald and golden eagles, otters, mink and bobcats, plus three endangered plants that grow nowhere else. Sadly it's also been hammered by more than a century of farming and building, but people have been restoring it since the 1990s.

And a nerdy little twist. Mark West Creek, which we followed down the hills, has been diverted in three places, so now it looks like the creek feeds the Laguna, when naturally it's the other way round. Sneaky.

Oh, and the tiny place you're passing is Fulton, founded by the brothers Thomas and James Fulton, with a post office since 1871.

clips.title: Meeting the Russian River
clips.text:
Woohoo! Welcome to the Russian River, everybody, the last leg of our journey. It's the second-biggest river in the Bay Area, 115 miles long, flowing south out of Mendocino County and then west to the Pacific.

Quiz! Why do you think a river in California is called the Russian River? … Because of actual Russians! In the early 1800s, the Russian-American Company ran a fur-trading colony at Fort Ross on the coast, and one of their explorers, Ivan Kuskov, travelled up this river. An 1817 Russian map calls it the Slavyanka. But long before that, the Southern Pomo called it Ashokawna, the east water place, and Bidapte, big river.

This is also the Russian River Valley wine region: cool, foggy country thanks to the nearby ocean, which is perfect for Pinot Noir and Chardonnay. By 1900 there were nearly 200 wineries around here. And before the vines? Redwoods, lining the banks. You'll see them close in as we head downstream. Get ready for the trees!

clips.title: California's first commercial sawmill
clips.text:
Here's a quick one. Right around here, near Forestville, was California's first commercial water-powered sawmill. It was built in 1834 by John Bautista Rogers Cooper, a sea captain who'd married General Vallejo's sister. The Mexican government gave him this land partly as a strategy: get settlers out here to keep an eye on the Russians at Fort Ross.

The mill ran on Mark West Creek and cut redwood. Quiz: how long do you think it survived? … About seven years! Floods destroyed it in the winter of 1840. The river always wins around here.

Forestville itself was settled in the late 1860s, originally spelled with two r's after one of its founders. And by 1900 it had a reputation as a hangout for bohemian writers and artists.

clips.title: Floods, dams and the river that borrows from the Eel
clips.text:
This lovely, lazy river has a wild side. Flood stage here at Guerneville is 32 feet. Quiz: the record flood, in February 1986, went way past that. How high do you think it got? … 49 and a half feet! Seventeen feet over flood stage. And in the second half of the twentieth century the river flooded about five times a decade. Two big dams upstream now hold back a lot of that water, but in February 2019 it got almost as high as in 1986.

And here's a water fight brewing. Some of this river's summer water doesn't even belong to it! Since 1908, a tunnel up in Mendocino County has been borrowing water from a totally different river, the Eel River, and sending it into the Russian. That borrowed water helps supply drinking water to more than 600,000 people in Sonoma and Marin. But in 2019 PG&E decided the old hydro plant wasn't worth keeping. The Eel River dams are going to be removed, and everyone downstream is trying to figure out how to keep some of that water coming.

clips.title: Korbel: Bohemian brothers and California champagne
clips.text:
Okay, wine lovers, up ahead is a winery that legally prints the word champagne on its labels, and France can't do anything about it.

It's Korbel, making sparkling wine here since 1882. It was started by Francis Korbel and his brothers, who came from Bohemia, and who also, randomly, started a satirical San Francisco magazine called The Wasp. They use the proper Champagne method, where the wine gets its second fermentation right in the bottle you buy.

So how do they get away with saying champagne? … Old American rules from the 1930s treat some place names as semi-generic, as long as the label also says where the grapes were really grown. And a 2006 deal with Europe protected older American brands that were already using it. Somewhere, a Frenchman is wincing. Korbel makes about 1.6 million cases a year now.

clips.title: Rio Nido: there is no Canyon Five
clips.text:
Here's one of my favourite little places: Rio Nido, the river nest, a tiny resort village tucked into a redwood canyon. It was started in 1908 by a San Francisco lodge called the Eagles, so its first name was Eaglenest. In World War Two, its dance hall was packed with sailors on leave and big bands played there.

Okay, Julia, Adam, here's a weird one. The streets here are named Canyon One, Canyon Two, Canyon Three, Canyon Four, then Canyon Six and Canyon Seven. What's missing? … There's no Canyon Five! The story goes it's because of an accident on the road that became Canyon Six. Spooky.

And the town's unofficial slogan? The Moon Is Always Out In Rio Nido. Love that.

clips.title: Guerneville: from Stumptown to resort town
clips.text:
Ladies and gentlemen, Julia, Adam and our amazing driver: welcome to Guerneville! You made it! Woohoo!

Okay, pronunciation check. It's Gurn-vill. Locals even sell T-shirts that say Don't call it Guerneyville. So now you know.

Final quiz of the trip. The town's very first English name was a bit less pretty. Given that loggers cut down most of the giant redwoods here in the late 1800s, what do you think they called it? … Stumptown! And the parade every year is still called Stumptown Days. The redwoods grew so thick here that local legend says the valley had the densest amount of living stuff on the planet. Then the loggers came, especially after the 1906 earthquake, when San Francisco needed rebuilding. Today's forests on the hills are mostly less than 200 years old, regrown after all that logging.

Before all of that, the local Pomo used this spot as a summer camp and called it Ceola, the shady place. The name Guerneville comes from George Guerne, a Swiss guy who owned the sawmill. In 1877 the railroad arrived and the town became San Francisco's summer playground. Then in the late seventies, gay entrepreneurs from San Francisco discovered it and brought it back to life, and it's been a famously welcoming town ever since.

Thanks for riding with me today, gang. You've been a great audience. Go enjoy those redwoods!

clips.title: Armstrong Redwoods: the trees the loggers missed
clips.text:
If you've got an hour, go see the trees that the loggers missed: Armstrong Redwoods, just north of town. In the 1870s, Colonel James Armstrong saved the grove as a natural park. After he died, his daughter and another local family ran a whole campaign, with rallies and car caravans, to save this last bit of the old forest, and in 1917 the county bought it for 80,000 dollars.

Quiz: the tallest tree in there, the Parson Jones Tree, is a hundred yards from the entrance. How tall do you think it is? … More than 310 feet! That's taller than a thirty-storey building. And the oldest, the Colonel Armstrong Tree, is over 1,400 years old. There's an easy trail through the grove, wheelchair-accessible too. Totally worth it.

clips.title: Bohemian Grove: the most exclusive campsite in America
clips.text:
Okay, conspiracy fans, this one's for you. Just downstream at Monte Rio, hidden in the redwoods, is the Bohemian Grove: a 2,700-acre private campground owned by San Francisco's very exclusive Bohemian Club. Every July, powerful people from politics, business and the arts spend more than two weeks camping here.

It started innocently. In 1878, a bunch of journalists from the club had an overnight going-away party in the redwoods for an actor moving to New York. They had so much fun they did it again the next year, without him! Then the rich businessmen joined, and the money and the power followed.

Quiz: in 1942, something top-secret was planned at the Grove. What do you think it was? … An early planning meeting for the Manhattan Project, the atomic bomb! And in 1950, Dwight Eisenhower and Richard Nixon met for the first time here, at a lunch hosted by Herbert Hoover.

No woman has ever been a full member. And the secrecy creates legends. In 2000, the broadcaster Alex Jones sneaked in, filmed the club's Cremation of Care ceremony, and called it a ritual sacrifice. Other reporting doesn't support that, and another filmmaker who saw the same footage said it looked more like an overgrown frat party. Fun fact: one of the camps inside is called Silverado Squatters, after Stevenson's book!

clips.title: The Pomo: the people of the Russian River
clips.text:
This river is Pomo country. The Pomo lands once stretched from the Pacific coast all the way inland to Clear Lake. But here's the thing: the Pomo were never one single nation. They lived in small, independent bands linked by family, and they spoke seven related languages so different that speakers of one couldn't understand another.

Quiz: the name Pomo was originally the name of just one village. What do you think it meant? … Those who live at red earth hole! Probably after the red magnesite they mined to make beads, or the reddish soil. By 1877, English speakers were using it for everyone.

The Southern Pomo, who lived along this lower river, were the first to be hit by Spanish colonisation, and were even used as labour to build the last of the California missions, in Sonoma. By 2012, there was just one fluent speaker of Southern Pomo left. But since 2011 the Dry Creek Rancheria has been bringing it back, with classes, a phone app, and signs on their ancestral land. And their old Coyote stories even mention the beavers that used to dam this river.

clips.title: Interstate 505: the highway that lost its letter
clips.text:
Fun fact: the road you've just turned onto used to have a letter in its number! This is Interstate 505, a quiet four-lane road running about thirty miles up the edge of the valley to Interstate 5. Basically, it lets people skip Sacramento entirely.

It was originally planned as part of a loop called I-5W, W for west. Then the feds scrapped almost all the lettered interstates and chopped I-5W into pieces. One piece became the stretch of I-80 you just drove, and this piece became 505. The northern end only opened in 1977.

That ridge to your left is the Vaca Mountains. The flat ground you're on is gravel and sand washed down out of them, plus a few patches of a layer called the Tehama Formation, old river mud and volcanic ash from a few million years ago.

clips.title: Winters: orchards on Putah Creek
clips.text:
Coming up is Winters, a cute little town on Putah Creek, right where it comes out of the hills. And it's one of the places where farming in the whole Sacramento Valley got started.

In 1842, a Kentucky guy named William Wolfskill was granted a ranch along this creek, and his brother John started planting orchards and vineyards here. He's credited with kicking off farming in the entire Sacramento Valley.

Quiz: the town is named Winters. Was that because of the weather? … Nope! It's named after Theodore Winters, whose ranch provided half the land for the town. Not very wintry at all. And in 1935, the Wolfskill family gave a hundred acres of the old ranch to UC Davis for an experimental orchard. Now we leave the freeway and follow Highway 128 west, up the creek, into the hills.

clips.title: Putah Creek: the creek that came back
clips.text:
See that creek next to the road? That's Putah Creek, and its name has caused some drama.

Quiz: the early spelling of this creek's name got rejected by the federal government. Why do you think? … It looked like a rude word in Spanish! Old maps spelled it Puta Creek, and the naming board said, no thank you. The experts say the resemblance is totally accidental, and the name actually comes from the Lake Miwok words for grassy creek. The Patwin call it Liwaito.

And it's a feel-good environmental story too. After a drought in the late 1980s, most of the creek below the dams dried up completely. That led to a big lawsuit, and in 2000 everybody signed the Putah Creek Accord, which guarantees water releases that copy the natural seasons. And it worked: the number of streamside bird species doubled, and native steelhead trout and Chinook salmon came back to spawn. While the farmers kept their water too. Everybody wins!

clips.title: Fire country on Highway 128
clips.text:
These dry, grassy canyons burn a lot. Highway 128 has been closed by fire again and again.

Quiz: in July 2015, the Wragg Fire started right next to this highway. What do you think started it? … The hot exhaust of an idling car touching dry grass. That's all it took. It forced 136 homes to evacuate and closed this road and the freeway. Then there was the Winters Fire in 2017, and the Quail Fire in 2020.

clips.title: Monticello Dam and the Glory Hole
clips.text:
Okay, look up the canyon! That's Monticello Dam, a 304-foot concrete arch jammed into a narrow gorge called Devil's Gate. It's a hundred feet thick at the bottom and only twelve at the top. And when they poured the last bucket of concrete in February 1957, the crew tossed in a few coins for luck.

But the coolest thing about it is hidden. Quiz: when the lake gets too full, how does the extra water get out? … Through the Glory Hole! It's a giant concrete funnel in the lake, 72 feet across, dropping 200 feet straight down through the hillside. When the lake's full, water pours into it like the world's biggest bathtub drain. It doesn't happen often: in 2017 it overflowed for the first time since 2006, then again in 2019. And it's genuinely dangerous: in 1997 a woman was pulled in and killed.

Behind the dam is Lake Berryessa, the biggest lake in Napa County, about sixteen miles long with 165 miles of shoreline. Fun detail: the dam and lake are completely in Napa County, but the dam is less than 500 feet from two other counties.

clips.title: Monticello: the town under the lake
clips.text:
Here's something kind of haunting. Under Lake Berryessa there's a whole town.

This valley used to be a ranch belonging to the Berryessa family, which is where the lake gets its name. They lost it fast. Quiz: by 1853 they owed a guy 1,645 dollars and couldn't pay. So the county auctioned off 26,000 acres. What do you think it sold for? … 2,000 dollars! And the buyer flipped it for 100,000. Brutal.

In 1866, developers laid out a town called Monticello. Farmers poured in, growing wheat and barley on what was considered some of the best soil in the country. It had hotels, blacksmiths, a general store, and in 1896 a beautiful three-arched stone bridge, the biggest stone bridge west of the Rockies.

Then in 1947 the government decided to build a dam. The residents protested, but the governor backed it, and the town was doomed. The famous photographer Dorothea Lange documented its death for Life magazine, although Life never ran the story. Buildings were knocked down, the cemetery was moved up to a bluff called Spanish Flat, and the post office closed in 1956. But that old stone bridge? It was built so well they couldn't easily demolish it. So they just left it. It's still down there, under the water.

clips.title: Driving through tilted sea floor
clips.text:
Okay, geology moment! Every road cut along here is a page from the bottom of a dinosaur-age sea.

The layered sandstone and shale you're passing is the Great Valley Sequence, the same old sea floor that's buried miles deep under the flat valley behind us. Here it comes up to the surface. The geological maps show formations with names like the Sites, the Venado and the Yolo. Near the dam, the Venado even has a layer of giant jumbled blocks at the bottom.

Quiz: how do geologists know how old the Yolo Formation is? … Microscopic fossils! Tiny sea creatures in the mudstone date it to the late Cretaceous, roughly 88 million years ago. Back then, sand and mud were pouring down underwater canyons off ancient volcanoes and settling on the deep ocean floor. So every time we pass a road cut, you're looking at the bottom of a sea from the age of the dinosaurs.

clips.title: Serpentine: the floor of an ancient ocean
clips.text:
Keep your eyes on the road cuts! Look for a colour change: greenish, shiny, slippery-looking rock, and thin, scrubby plants. That's something pretty rare.

The geological maps say this stretch of Highway 128 crosses the Coast Range Ophiolite. Quiz: an ophiolite is a slab of something you're normally never supposed to see on land. Any idea what? … The ocean floor! An ophiolite is a chunk of ocean crust, plus a piece of the Earth's mantle underneath it, shoved up onto a continent. The rock here started as peridotite, which comes from the mantle, and seawater forced deep into it turned it into serpentinite. This slab is Jurassic, and it's called arguably the biggest ophiolite in the United States.

And the soil from it is tough on plants: low in calcium, high in heavy metals like chromium and nickel. That's why the slopes look so bare, and why the area is home to rare plants that grow nowhere else.

clips.title: Berryessa Snow Mountain: a monument without its lake
clips.text:
Here's a national monument that deliberately left out its own lake. Because of jet skis!

The wild hills around Lake Berryessa are part of the Berryessa Snow Mountain National Monument, created by President Obama in July 2015. It stretches about a hundred miles north into Mendocino County, with bald and golden eagles, black bears, mountain lions and tule elk. And people have lived in these hills for around 11,000 years: Patwin, Pomo, Wappo, Lake Miwok, Yuki and more.

A whole coalition of counties, cities, a Pomo tribe and conservation groups campaigned for it. But boaters worried that a national monument might one day ban their motorboats and jet skis, so the lake was left out. Then in May 2024, President Biden added nearly 14,000 acres, including an eleven-mile ridge called Molok Luyuk.

clips.title: The Franciscan Complex: California's geological junk drawer
clips.text:
Okay, here's California's geological junk drawer: the Franciscan Complex, and much of the Coast Ranges from here to the ocean is made of it.

For tens of millions of years, an ocean plate was diving under North America, and as it went down, it scraped off a crazy mix of stuff: deep-sea sandstone, chert full of tiny fossils, ocean-floor basalt, and chunks of rock that got dragged deep underground, squeezed under enormous pressure, then popped back up. Geologists call it an accretionary wedge, and the Franciscan is the textbook example.

Quiz: there's a rock in here called mélange. That's French for mixture. What do you think it looks like? … A fruitcake! Blocks of chert, greenstone, serpentinite and blueschist floating in a squished, muddy matrix. And blueschist is a rare blue rock that only forms deep in a subduction zone, at high pressure but low temperature. So if you spot a blue-grey shiny rock in a road cut later today, you might be looking at old ocean floor that went down into the Earth and somehow came back. And look closely at the geology maps: these hills are dotted with mapped landslides.

clips.title: Lake Hennessey and the valleys behind the hills
clips.text:
This little lake lent its name to the fire at the heart of California's seventh-largest wildfire complex. Here's the story.

This is Lake Hennessey, the City of Napa's main water supply. Congress approved a dam here in 1944 but never paid for it, so in 1946 the city just built it themselves, for 550,000 dollars. It's named after Edwin Hennessey, a local leader who helped get it done.

Early on the morning of the 17th of August 2020, a lightning strike started a small fire on Hennessey Ridge Road near the lake. The Hennessey Fire grew to 192,000 acres all by itself, the heart of the LNU Lightning Complex.

Now a fun one. Hidden in the hills to the north is Pope Valley. Quiz: a scene from a James Bond movie was filmed in the sky above it in 1978. Which movie? … Moonraker! The opening skydiving sequence. Not bad for a sleepy little valley. Nearby is Chiles Valley too, where Joseph Chiles planted vines back in 1850.

clips.title: Who gets the water? The Solano Project
clips.text:
California's history is basically a history of moving water around, and Lake Berryessa is a textbook case.

The farms of Solano and Yolo counties had been worked since the 1840s, but the summers were bone-dry. As early as 1907, Bay Area cities hired a group of engineers to look at damming Putah Creek, but they moved on to bigger projects. Then in 1947, the county and the federal Bureau of Reclamation launched the Solano Project, with Governor Earl Warren pushing hard, to water 96,000 acres of prime farmland.

Quiz: Lake Berryessa can hold 1.6 million acre-feet of water. How much do you think flows in each year? … About 375,000 acre-feet. So refilling it from empty would take more than four years' worth of inflow. Downstream, a smaller dam sends water through a canal to farms and to the taps of Vallejo and Benicia.

The cost fell on the people of the valley, who lost their whole town, and on the creek itself, which ran dry below the dams in the late eighties until the lawyers sorted it out in 2000. It's a small version of the deal behind every big California water project: the cities and farms win, somebody's valley gets flooded, and the fish wait for the lawyers.

clips.title: Los Carneros: the land of the rams

Which explains the fancy French château on the hill: Domaine Carneros, started in 1987 by the Champagne house Taittinger, and modelled on their own château in France.

clips.title: di Rosa: moonshine, mushrooms and modern art
clips.text:
Hidden off this road is the di Rosa art centre, and the land has had quite a life.

In 1855 someone planted grapes and olives here. In 1886 two Frenchmen built a stone winery. Then the phylloxera bug killed the vines, and the old winery got used for growing mushrooms, making moonshine, storing grain, and finally as a hay barn.

In 1960, Rene di Rosa bought it, replanted vines and turned an old Depression-era pond into a 35-acre lake. When he sold the vineyards in 1986, he used the money to turn the whole place into an art park. Now it has about 1,600 works by Northern California artists, in galleries and a sculpture meadow, and the land is protected forever.

clips.title: Bliss: the most famous hill in the world
clips.text:
Okay, this is one of my all-time favourite stories. Julia, Adam: did you ever use a computer with Windows XP? Picture the default desktop picture. … The green hill and the blue sky! It's called Bliss, and it might be the most viewed photograph in history. And it was taken right around here, near the Napa-Sonoma county line, on this very highway.

In January 1996, a former National Geographic photographer, Charles O'Rear, who lived in St. Helena, was driving to see his girlfriend. A storm had just passed, the winter rain had turned the grass bright green, and he spotted a hill that had been cleared of vines because of the phylloxera bug. He pulled over, set up his tripod, and took four shots. And he says he didn't edit it at all.

Microsoft bought the full rights in 2000. People have tried to recreate the shot ever since, but they can't. Quiz: why not? … The hill went back to being a vineyard! So look out for green hills with vines on them. One of them is the most famous hill in the world, wearing a disguise.

clips.title: Schellville junction and a quarter-scale railroad
clips.text:
This crossroads is Schellville, and it's got two railroads: a real one that floods, and a quarter-size one that one guy built by himself.

The real one first. Schellville has been a rail junction since 1888, with a two-mile railyard. Being low by Sonoma Creek, it floods every five to ten years. And in March 2023, after months of rain, the soggy ground gave way and a train full of corn seed derailed right here. Nobody was hurt.

Now the fun one. On the way into Sonoma is Sonoma TrainTown. Stanley Frank from Oakland started building it in 1958, and he made everything himself: the tiny houses, the landscaping, even the steam engines. Everything is exactly one quarter of real size. It opened in 1968, and his family still runs it: a twenty-minute ride past waterfalls and tiny houses, over a trestle and through tunnels, on four miles of track.

clips.title: Sonoma: the last mission and the largest plaza
clips.text:
Welcome to Sonoma, where modern California kind of began!

Quiz: Spain built a famous chain of twenty-one missions along California. This town has the very last one, and the northernmost. And it's the only one not built by the Spanish. Who built it? … Mexico! Mission San Francisco Solano was founded in 1823, just after Mexico won independence. And part of the reason was to keep an eye on the Russians at Fort Ross. Russians again!

When Mexico shut down the missions in the 1830s, a young officer called Mariano Guadalupe Vallejo was sent to turn this one into a town. In 1835 he laid out the plaza you'll see in the middle, the biggest town plaza in California. And the City Hall in the middle of it, dedicated in 1908, was built with four identical sides, so none of the shopkeepers around the square would feel snubbed. How diplomatic is that?

clips.title: The Blue Wing Inn: a gold-rush hotel with a gambling hall
clips.text:

It started with the very first property deal in the new town: Vallejo gave the lot to his manager, Antonio Ortega. The local priest soon complained about how Ortega treated the Native people, and after more scandals and some dodgy accounts, Vallejo fired him in 1837. Ortega stayed on anyway and ran a tavern there.

Then in 1849, in the middle of the Gold Rush, two guys bought it and turned it into a hotel, with a gambling hall and a saloon, serving miners heading to and from the gold fields and the American soldiers stationed here. Wild West vibes.

clips.title: The Bear Flag Revolt: a republic that lasted 25 days
clips.text:
Okay, here's California's strangest little rebellion, and it happened right on Sonoma's plaza.

By 1846, Mexico had pretty much ignored California for years, and Mexican officials were nervous about all the Americans showing up uninvited. Those Americans, in turn, complained they couldn't buy land and were being threatened with getting kicked out.

So, early on the morning of the 14th of June 1846, about thirty-three American settlers rode into Sonoma and took General Vallejo prisoner. Here's the funny part: Vallejo actually liked the idea of American rule! He sat down to negotiate his own surrender, while, according to accounts, the rebels proceeded to get drunk. They raised a homemade flag with a grizzly bear and the words California Republic, and declared independence.

Quiz: how long do you think the California Republic lasted? … About three and a half weeks! The Mexican-American War had already broken out, and on the 9th of July a U.S. Navy lieutenant raised the American flag in front of the Sonoma barracks, and that was that. But the bear flag survived: it became the basis of California's state flag. There's a monument on the plaza where it was first raised.

clips.title: General Vallejo: the man in the middle
clips.text:
Okay, one man pops up in almost every story on this side of the hills: Mariano Guadalupe Vallejo. Let's meet him properly.

He was born in Monterey in 1807, the eighth of thirteen kids of a Spanish soldier. As a boy he got private lessons from the governor, with access to his library, and an English merchant taught him English, French and Latin. clips.title: The Count of Buena Vista and the birth of California wine
clips.text:
Sonoma Valley calls itself the birthplace of the California wine industry, and here's the colourful guy who helps make that case: Agoston Haraszthy.

A Hungarian nobleman and adventurer, he'd already founded a village in Wisconsin, where the German settlers called him the Count, and been the first sheriff of San Diego. Then in 1857, just east of Sonoma, he founded Buena Vista, one of California's first successful commercial wineries. He's often called the father of California wine, and he brought in more than 300 kinds of European grapes. His money skills were less impressive, though. The bankers had to take over, and he was pushed out in 1866.

Next door, a Bavarian, Jacob Gundlach, planted a vineyard in 1858 called Rhinefarm. Gundlach Bundschu is now the oldest winery in California owned by the same family the whole time, six generations!

Quiz: when that nasty phylloxera bug was destroying vineyards all over California in the late 1800s, someone here in the Sonoma Valley figured out the fix. What was it? … Grafting European vines onto tough, disease-resistant American roots. A grower called Julius Dresel did it first, commercially, and it saved the entire California wine industry.

clips.title: The Springs: hot water and Guadalcanal veterans
clips.text:
In 1943, ninety veterans of Guadalcanal were sent to a fancy resort here to recover with golf, cherry pie and dances. Here's the story.

North of Sonoma, the highway runs through a string of little towns known as the Springs: Boyes Hot Springs, Fetters Hot Springs, Agua Caliente and El Verano. Agua Caliente means hot water, and Native people used and considered these springs sacred long before anyone else showed up.

Quiz: in 1895, a Captain Boyes drilled down just 70 feet. What did he hit? … 112-degree hot water! He built a resort hotel, which burned down in a wildfire in 1923. Its replacement became the Sonoma Mission Inn. And in World War Two, the Navy borrowed it as a rest centre for sailors and Marines back from the Pacific, including those Guadalcanal veterans. From one of the worst battles in history, straight to soft beds and cherry pie.

clips.title: Eldridge: the dark history of the Sonoma Developmental Center
clips.text:
This one's a darker story, but an important one. Off to the west, near the village of Eldridge, are the grounds of the Sonoma Developmental Center, which for over a century was a big state institution for people with developmental disabilities. It opened here in 1891.

California passed a forced sterilisation law in 1909, only the third state to do so. From 1918, the superintendent here, F. O. Butler, was a big believer in it, and personally performed at least a thousand operations. The centre even admitted people just to sterilise them and send them home. It was said to have sterilised more people than any other institution in the world, and risky medical experiments on residents went on into the 1960s.

It finally closed at the end of 2018. Not every story on a road trip is a happy one, but this one's worth knowing.

clips.title: Jack London and the Valley of the Moon
clips.text:
Up on the slopes of Sonoma Mountain, above the village of Glen Ellen, is the ranch of Jack London, and his life was as wild as his books.

Born in San Francisco in 1876, he was an oyster pirate in the bay as a teenager, sailed off to the Klondike gold rush at 21, and came back a committed socialist. Quiz: in 1903 he sold The Call of the Wild, one of the most famous books ever, to a magazine. How much do you think he got for it? … 750 dollars!

In 1905 he bought an abandoned winery here and called it Beauty Ranch. Then he started building his dream house, Wolf House: 26 rooms, nine fireplaces, built of massive stone to survive earthquakes, with fancy new stuff like electric lights, refrigeration and even a built-in vacuum cleaner. He and his wife Charmian spent over 80,000 dollars on it. And then, on the 22nd of August 1913, just before they were due to move in, it burned down.

He was devastated, deep in debt, and he died at the ranch in 1916, aged just forty. His ashes are under a rock from the ruins of Wolf House. He also wrote a novel called The Valley of the Moon, a translation of the Native name for the Sonoma Valley. You can still walk to the stone ruins today.
