clips.title: Volcanic glass of the Valley of the Moon
clips.text:
Here's something you could find in the gravel around here: natural volcanic glass!

The geology maps around Glen Ellen and Kenwood show a layer called the Glen Ellen Formation: river gravel made mostly of eroded volcanic rock, famous for its pebbles of obsidian. Up in the hills there's a lava called the Rhyolite of Adobe Canyon, glassy and grey-white with swirly folded bands, about 5.3 million years old.

Nearby Annadel State Park's whole history is written in this rock: Native Americans used its obsidian, and then, quiz, in the early 1900s people quarried its volcanic rock for something you've definitely walked on. What? … Cobblestones! And some biologists say Annadel has the best untouched oak woodland anywhere.

clips.title: Kenwood: the town that couldn't pick a name
clips.text:
This next town tried on more names than a teenager tries on outfits.

Kenwood sits on an old Mexican ranch called Los Guilicos, granted in 1837 to a Scottish sea captain who never even lived on it. In 1850 he sold it to another Scot, William Hood, a cabinet-maker who'd climbed the mountain above the valley, fallen in love with the view, and made his fortune building houses in Gold Rush San Francisco to afford it. The mountain's now called Hood Mountain.

When the railroad arrived in 1887, the town tried Rohrerville, then Los Guilicos, then South Los Guilicos. Quiz: why do you think people wanted to change it again? … Nobody could pronounce Guilicos! So around 1895 they voted for Kenwood. Either because settlers came from Kenwood in Illinois, or because English families knew Kenwood House in London. Maybe both!

Up to the north-east is Sugarloaf Ridge State Park. When the state planned to close it in 2011 to save money, a group of volunteers called Team Sugarloaf took it over and reopened it. They even run an observatory up there.

clips.title: Santa Rosa: the slaughtering place and the Carrillo adobe
clips.text:
Welcome to Santa Rosa, the biggest city in California's wine country! And it has a creek with a pretty grim name. Let me explain.

Before Europeans arrived, the Santa Rosa plain belonged to a powerful Pomo group called the Bitakomtara. They controlled it tightly: outsiders needed permission to pass through, and if they didn't ask, the penalties were harsh. They gathered for ceremonies on Santa Rosa Creek, near today's Spring Lake. Colonisation brought violence, enslavement and smallpox, and devastated them, though their descendants still live in the region.

The first European home here was built in the 1830s by María López de Carrillo, a widow from San Diego, whose daughter had married General Vallejo. Quiz: before she arrived, settlers from Sonoma used to slaughter cattle where two creeks meet, and one creek got named after it. Matanza means what in Spanish? … Slaughter! So that's Matanzas Creek. Lovely. In the 1850s her son helped lay out the downtown grid around a central square, and the city still follows it.

clips.title: Luther Burbank: the plant wizard of Santa Rosa
clips.text:
Near downtown Santa Rosa is the house and garden of Luther Burbank, one of the most famous plant breeders who ever lived. And Julia, Adam, there's a really good chance you've eaten his work.

He was born in Massachusetts in 1849, the thirteenth of fifteen kids. As a young man he bred a new potato, sold the rights for 150 dollars, and used the money to move to Santa Rosa in 1875. Inspired by Charles Darwin, he crossed plants on an enormous scale and created more than 800 varieties: the Shasta daisy, the Santa Rosa plum, a white blackberry, a spineless cactus for cattle.

Quiz: a natural variant of his potato became the most widely grown potato in the United States. And a big share of one very famous fast-food chain's french fries are made from it. Which chain? … McDonald's! The Russet Burbank is the classic french fry potato. So next time you have McDonald's fries, say thanks to Luther. He's buried in his garden here, under a cedar tree.

clips.title: Charles Schulz, Snoopy and the ice rink
clips.text:

In 1969 he and his wife built an ice rink here, and everyone calls it Snoopy's Home Ice. Quiz: what do you think the café inside the rink is called? … The Warm Puppy! Every summer it hosts Snoopy's Senior World Hockey Tournament for older players from around the world.

Down the street is the Charles M. Schulz Museum, with a 22-foot mural made of 3,588 Peanuts comic strips that together make a picture of Lucy holding the football for Charlie Brown.

And here's my favourite Santa Rosa coincidence. Schulz's very first published drawing, in 1937, was of his family dog Spike, who ate pins, tacks and razor blades. He sent it to Ripley's Believe It or Not, and they ran it! And Robert Ripley, who created Believe It or Not? Born right here in Santa Rosa.

clips.title: Believe It or Not: Robert Ripley of Santa Rosa

He left high school after his dad died, started drawing sports cartoons for newspapers at sixteen, and moved to New York in 1913. He took his facts seriously enough to hire a full-time researcher. And by 1929 the panel was running in 360 newspapers in 17 languages, followed by radio and TV shows. Quiz: Ripley also held a sports title. Which sport? … Handball! He was New York State handball champion in 1926. Believe it or not. A perfect Santa Rosan for a day full of oddities.

clips.title: The Rodgers Creek Fault: the Hayward Fault's northern half
clips.text:
Okay, a little earthquake talk. Somewhere under this part of Santa Rosa runs one of the most dangerous faults in the Bay Area.

You've probably heard of the Hayward Fault, under Berkeley and Oakland. Well, this side of the bay has its partner: the Rodgers Creek Fault, running right through Santa Rosa. In 2016 scientists showed the two are actually connected under San Pablo Bay, making one fault about 120 miles long, from north of Healdsburg all the way to San Jose. It's the kind of fault where the ground on the other side slides sideways, to your right.

Quiz: on the evening of the 1st of October 1969, Santa Rosa got hit by not one, but how many earthquakes, about an hour and twenty minutes apart? … Two! Magnitude 5.6 and 5.7. Chimneys fell, sidewalks buckled, pipes burst, and one person died. The damage was worse than expected, and modelling suggests the city sits where a basin full of sediment amplifies the shaking. Luckily it was evening, so few people were on the streets. Afterwards the city started earthquake-proofing its old brick buildings.

clips.title: Knights Valley: a Mexican soldier's hunting preserve
clips.text:
Over the hill from Calistoga, Highway 128 drops into Knights Valley, a small, quiet valley with the warmest climate in Sonoma County.

In 1843 the Mexican governor rewarded a soldier from the Sonoma garrison, José de los Santos Berreyesa, with almost 18,000 acres, which included this valley and even the hot springs at Calistoga. Quiz: what do you think he used this beautiful valley for? … His own private hunting preserve! And the adobe hunting lodge he built is still standing.

The English name comes from Thomas Knight, a guy from Maine who'd been one of the Bear Flag rebels in Sonoma in 1846. He bought a big chunk of the ranch, and his name stuck.

clips.text:

Quiz: so what's the white stuff in the soil really? … Volcanic ash! White tuff, from the eruptions of the Mount Saint Helena area, the same volcanism that turned the Petrified Forest to stone. It's said to be great for white grapes, and there's a warm band of air here, so harvest often comes in September, weeks before the neighbours.

A bit further on, along Alexander Valley Road, the maps show a basalt lava flow and that obsidian-studded Glen Ellen gravel again. These are some of the last outposts of the big volcanic field, before the land turns to the old sea-floor rocks closer to the coast.

clips.title: Alexander Valley: Kit Carson's brother and the Wappo name
clips.text:
You're entering the Alexander Valley, the big, vine-filled valley of the Russian River north of Healdsburg. It's the largest and most fully planted wine region in Sonoma County, with more than a hundred wineries.

The story starts with a ranch called Sotoyome, almost 49,000 acres, named after a Wappo group. It went to Henry Fitch, a San Diego sea captain who was General Vallejo's brother-in-law. Fitch never lived here. He hired a manager, Cyrus Alexander, with a deal that after four years, Alexander would get a chunk of land and some cattle. Alexander settled down, and the valley took his name, even though the American land commission later rejected his claim to it. Ouch.

Quiz: Alexander's replacement as ranch manager was the brother of a very famous Wild West frontiersman. Who? … Kit Carson! His brother Mose Carson ran the ranch after 1845.

And a wine note: Jordan winery here, with its French-style château from 1976, had a long-time winemaker who was trained by André Tchelistcheff, the Beaulieu legend from Rutherford.

clips.title: Healdsburg: a squatter's town and the birthplace of lemon pepper
clips.text:
Healdsburg is named after a squatter, and it gave the world lemon pepper. Seriously.

It sits on the Russian River where three famous wine regions meet: the Alexander Valley, the Dry Creek Valley and the Russian River Valley. The Pomo built villages along the river here. The name comes from Harmon Heald, an Ohio businessman who squatted on the land from 1850, then bought a piece of it in 1857 when the owners auctioned off land to pay their taxes. The railroad arrived in 1872. And when Prohibition shut the wineries of Dry Creek Valley, which had been one of California's top Zinfandel regions, a lot of the land was switched to plums and prunes.

Quiz: what famous seasoning was first developed commercially here in 1967? It's in the title. … Lemon pepper! Thanks, Healdsburg.

If you cross the old steel bridge into town, that's the Healdsburg Memorial Bridge from 1921, one of only thirteen bridges of its design in the whole country. People have been crossing the river at this exact spot since the 1850s, and the beach next to it is still a favourite swimming spot.

clips.title: Isabelle Simi, a winery that outlasted Prohibition, and Lytton
clips.text:
Here's a strong woman for you: Isabelle Simi. Simi Winery was started in San Francisco in 1876 by two Italian brothers who'd come for the Gold Rush, and they moved it here in 1881, paying 2,250 dollars in gold coins. From 1904, Giuseppe Simi's daughter Isabelle ran it, and she kept making wine right through Prohibition, storing it in the stone cellars. clips.title: Windsor: blackbird field and a Pony Express postmaster
clips.text:
Quiz: the town of Windsor, coming up, got its name from a Pony Express rider. Why do you think he chose Windsor? … He thought the countryside looked like the grounds of Windsor Castle, back in his home country of England! He was Hiram Lewis, the first postmaster, in 1855. Long before that, it was a Southern Pomo village called Tsoliikawai, which means blackbird field.

Windsor had a rough start to the 1900s: a fire wiped out the town centre in 1905, then the 1906 earthquake damaged buildings that were still being repaired. In World War Two, the army built an air base on the south side of town, now the Charles M. Schulz airport. And in 1943 there was even a camp here for German prisoners of war.

clips.title: Westside Road: blueschist and Pinot Noir
clips.text:
Westside Road is one of the prettiest drives in wine country, winding along the river through some of the most celebrated Pinot Noir country in California. Cool, foggy, gorgeous.

But check out the rocks too. The geology maps show this road crossing old sea-floor sandstone that got dragged down into the Earth in a subduction zone, squeezed at huge pressure, and turned blue with a mineral called glaucophane, then somehow made it back to the surface. It's called blueschist, and it's rare all over the world. Quiz: why do you think it's so rare? … Because it can only form deep in a subduction zone, and then it has to find its way all the way back up to the surface. Further along you'll pass mélange, that fruitcake rock, and old river gravels on flat benches cut into the bedrock.

So on this lovely, winding road, you're driving over bits of an ancient ocean floor that went down into the Earth and came back up.

clips.title: Sebastopol: a bar fight and the Gravenstein apple
clips.text:
Welcome to Sebastopol, which has one of the best name stories on the map. Quiz: the town was originally called Pine Grove. Then in the late 1850s, a bar fight broke out. And somehow that led to the new name. How? … A bystander said the long, drawn-out brawl was like the siege of Sevastopol, a Russian port in the Crimean War. And the name stuck! Remember Yountville? It was going to be called Sebastopol too, but this town got there first.

The Coast Miwok and Pomo were here first, and the town sits on top of several of their village sites. Later there was a busy Chinatown downtown from the 1880s.

Then came the apples. Sebastopol called itself the Gravenstein Apple Capital of the World. The Gravenstein is an old Danish apple, from the 1600s or earlier: tart, juicy, perfect for apple sauce and cider, but it doesn't keep, so you can only get it in season. There's still a Gravenstein Apple Fair every August. These days the old apple warehouses have turned into The Barlow, full of tasting rooms and restaurants.

clips.title: Burbank's Gold Ridge farm and the electric railway
clips.text:
Luther Burbank, our potato guy, needed more space than his Santa Rosa garden, so in 1885 he bought a farm here in the Gold Ridge area. Quiz: at its peak, how many plant experiments do you think he had going on this farm at once? … Over 60,000, by some estimates! Three acres of it survive, with more than 250 of his plants, looked after entirely by volunteers.

And Sebastopol used to have electric trolleys! From 1903 to 1947, the Petaluma and Santa Rosa Railway ran around the county, partly to break the big railroad's monopoly. All that's left is one passenger car in a museum, and its old stone power house on Petaluma Avenue, which has, very fittingly, been turned into a series of brew pubs.

clips.title: Sebastopol's sea-floor sandstone
clips.text:
Here's a surprise for a town twenty miles from the ocean. The geology maps show that Highway 116 north of Sebastopol runs for more than ten kilometres across an old sea floor! It's called the Wilson Grove Formation: pale sandstone laid down in the sea between about eleven and three million years ago, and in places it's full of broken-up seashells.

So all this gentle Gold Ridge country around Sebastopol used to be under the ocean, and got lifted up as the Coast Ranges rose. To the east, the Santa Rosa plain is made of gravel washed out of the hills. And as we head north toward the river, the road crosses into much older, harder rock from that geological junk drawer, the Franciscan Complex.

clips.title: Graton: the edge of the Russian empire
clips.text:
Graton, just off the highway, is a little apple town that turned into a wine town. And quiz: it was once at the very edge of an empire. Which one? … The Russian Empire! Graton is about as far south and east as Russian colonisation in the Americas ever reached. The Russians at Fort Ross on the coast needed food, so in 1836 their farm expert, Yegor Chernykh, set up a farm between here and Occidental, with barracks, vegetables, wheat, and a big vineyard. So Russians helped plant some of the first vines around here!

There's a sadder story in these hills too. In 1851, many California tribes signed treaties promising them land, but the U.S. never ratified them. In 1920 the government bought fifteen acres near here for the homeless Coast Miwok and Pomo people of the area. When seventy-five people tried to move in, they found only three acres were livable. And in 1958, the government ended the rancheria altogether.

clips.title: Freestone: the innkeeper who burned the bridge
clips.text:
Freestone, population about thirty-two, is the gateway to the Bohemian Highway. It's named after a sandstone quarry, and it was the first historic district Sonoma County ever named, in 1974.

And it has my favourite crime story of the trip. In 1876, a farmer built the Hinds Hotel here when he heard the railroad was coming, and the carpenters building the railway line stayed there. Quiz: according to first-hand reports, the innkeeper came up with a sneaky plan to keep his guests around longer. What did he do? … He had parts of the bridge they were building secretly burned at night, so the job would take longer! He went to jail for it. Customer retention, Wild West style.

And in the 1970s, the old hotel was the party headquarters for the artists Christo and Jeanne-Claude while they built their famous Running Fence.

clips.title: Occidental: Dutch Bill, sawmills and a commune deeded to God
clips.text:
This next town has a creek named after a sailor who jumped ship, and a commune that tried to give its land to God. Welcome to Occidental!

It was founded in 1876 as a stop on a railroad from the Sausalito ferry up to the redwoods. A local landowner, a Danish sailor known as Dutch Bill Howard, who'd jumped ship in San Francisco Bay in 1849, gave the railroad its right-of-way. In return he got a free lifetime train pass, and the station was named after him. The creek next to the road is still Dutch Bill Creek. The railroad started a timber boom, and by 1877 there were six sawmills here.

Then, a hundred years later: hippies! In 1966 Lou Gottlieb, from the folk band the Limeliters, bought land near here, and in 1967 he opened it to anyone who wanted to live there. Morning Star Ranch drew hundreds of people from San Francisco's Haight-Ashbury, and the county answered with arrests and bulldozers. Quiz: in 1969, Gottlieb tried to transfer the land to a new owner, to get the county off his back. Who? … God! He deeded the land to God. The courts did not accept God as the owner.

clips.title: Camp Meeker: the logger's subdivision
clips.text:
Quiz: how much would you pay for a plot of land twenty-five feet by twelve, with a one-room cabin on it? … In 1898, right here, it cost seventy-five dollars. This is Camp Meeker, named after Melvin Cyrus Meeker, a lumber baron who opened mills here around 1866. These redwoods built San Francisco, and then, after 1906, rebuilt it. Meeker is the same guy who sold the Bohemian Grove land to the Bohemian Club. Once the trees were cut down, he chopped the land into those tiny lots and sold them to San Franciscans wanting a summer escape.

Now it's a little village of about 425 people tucked among the new redwoods, with some roads so steep and narrow they feel like old railway tracks. And the creek has become a happy conservation story: wild coho salmon came back to spawn in 2001, young salmon have been released here since 2006, and in 2009 an old swimming-hole dam, one of the worst salmon blockers in the whole watershed, was swapped for a footbridge.

clips.title: The Coast Miwok
clips.text:
The land from the Golden Gate up to the Sonoma coast, and east to Sonoma Creek, was home to the Coast Miwok. That includes the hills around Sebastopol and Freestone and the lower Sonoma Valley.

They lived in small bands with no central government. In spring they headed to the coast for salmon, shellfish and seaweed. The rest of the year, acorns were the staple, plus deer and rabbit. Quiz: Coast Miwok hunters had a clever trick for sneaking up on deer. What do you think they did? … They rubbed themselves with a plant called Brewer's angelica to hide their scent! They also drank yerba buena tea as medicine, made tattoo ink from burned poison oak, and built cone-shaped houses called kotcha from tule reeds or redwood bark. Amazing basket makers too.

The word Miwok just means people. Within a couple of generations of the Spanish arriving, the people of this region lost their land and were devastated by disease. Later, broken federal treaties left them landless. If you ever visit Point Reyes, there's a recreated Coast Miwok village there called Kule Loklo.

clips.title: The Silverado Trail: cinnabar, Black Bart and a marathon
clips.text:
You're on the Silverado Trail, the quieter road up the east side of the Napa Valley, 29 miles long. And quiz: back in the 1880s, travellers on this road had to watch out for a famous someone. Who? … A stagecoach robber called Black Bart! He preyed on travellers here. Things got safer when a motor bus service started in 1910.

The road started in 1852 as a trail used when floods made the main valley road impassable. Later it became the wagon road for the mercury mines on Mount Saint Helena, and the first permanent road between Napa and Calistoga. Silver was found in the valley in 1858. Today there are at least forty wineries along it, and every March it hosts the Napa Valley Marathon.

The hills just east of Napa are called Coombsville, after Nathan Coombs, the guy who founded Napa. Volcanic soil, and fog that rolls in early and hangs around late.

clips.title: Stags Leap: the Cabernet that beat Bordeaux
clips.text:
Okay, wine fans, sit up! You're about to pass the vineyard that beat the French. This is the Stags Leap District, a tiny pocket of land only about one mile by three, with hills on three sides.

Here's the story. Warren Winiarski fell in love with wine while spending a year in Italy studying Machiavelli. He moved his family to Napa in 1968 and worked at Robert Mondavi's new winery. Then he tasted a homemade wine from a neighbour, Nathan Fay, and thought, this is it. In 1970 he bought the 44 acres next door. Quiz: what was growing on the land when he bought it? … Prunes, cherries and walnuts! He ripped them out and planted Cabernet. And his 1973 Cabernet went to Paris in 1976 and took first place, beating Château Mouton-Rothschild and Haut-Brion. The magazine Decanter called it a victory that put California on the winemaking map.

And the soil here is special: clay from the Napa River mixed with volcanic stuff washed down from the Vaca Mountains.

clips.title: Frog's Leap and Joe Heitz: jokes, organics and the turning point
clips.text:
Two wineries along here tell two sides of the Napa story.

First, Frog's Leap, started in 1981 by a doctor and a winemaker at a spot known as Frog Farm. Quiz: the winemaker got his start at a very famous winery nearby. Can you guess which, from the name? … Stag's Leap! Frog Farm plus Stag's Leap equals Frog's Leap. And the corks say Ribbit. But behind the jokes, it's serious stuff: it was the first Napa winery to use certified organic grapes, the vines aren't irrigated, and since 2005 solar panels supply most of its power.

Then Heitz Cellar, from 1961, back when Napa had only about two dozen wineries left. Joe Heitz, a farm boy from Illinois, was one of the first seven people ever to graduate from UC Davis in winemaking, in 1951. He trained under the legendary Tchelistcheff, bought a little vineyard for 5,000 dollars, and his Martha's Vineyard Cabernet became a Napa legend. It was even one of the reds tasted in Paris in 1976.

clips.text:
Mark Twain and Clark Gable both came to soak in springs near here. Near St. Helena was White Sulphur Springs, said to be the oldest warm-spring resort in Northern California, opened in 1852. Native people used the springs long before that.

In the late 1800s, rich San Franciscans got here by steamboat, then train, then stagecoach. Quiz: at its peak, how many guests could the grand hotel hold? … A thousand! clips.text:
You're climbing Spring Mountain Road into the Mayacamas. Quiz: where's the actual Spring Mountain? … Trick question! There isn't one. Spring Mountain was the name for a whole green, well-watered area of hills full of springs and little streams, not one peak.

It was one of the first places in Napa recognised for grapes. The first documented vineyard was Charles Lemme's La Perla, planted in 1874, and in the 1880s the Beringer brothers planted up here too. clips.title: The Mayacamas: a range that couldn't agree on its name
clips.text:
You're crossing a mountain range that the federal government couldn't decide how to spell! These are the Mayacamas Mountains, 52 miles long, separating the Napa and Sonoma valleys. The highest point is Cobb Mountain, 4,724 feet, and the rain that falls up here ends up in Putah Creek, Sonoma Creek, Santa Rosa Creek and Mark West Creek.

The name probably comes from a Wappo village called Maiya'kma, near Calistoga. Quiz: the federal naming board made one decision on the spelling, then reversed it in 1941. Which spelling did they finally pick? … Mayacmas! Without the second a. And plenty of people still write Mayacamas. And there's still a creek called Maacama. So, honestly, spell it however you like.

The road you're on crosses a volcanic landscape: white pumice from an eruption about 4.84 million years ago, grey lava from about 7.9 million, and swirly glassy lava from about 5.3 million. And about ten million years ago, these mountains were probably covered in cypress forest.

Which spelling did they finally pick? [[pause 5]] Mayacmas! Without the second a. And plenty of people still write My-uh-kah-muss. And there's still a creek called Mah-kah-muh. And about ten million years ago, these mountains were probably covered in cypress forest.

clips.title: Who gets to say Calistoga? The politics of wine labels
clips.text:
Two wineries went to war with the federal government over one word: Calistoga!

Here's the deal. Official wine regions are created by the federal government, and once one exists, wineries have to use mostly grapes from that area to put its name on the label. In 2003, Bo Barrett of Chateau Montelena asked for a Calistoga wine region. But two wineries, Calistoga Cellars and Calistoga Estate, already had Calistoga in their brand names. Quiz: what do you think they'd have to do if the region was approved? … Either use at least 85 percent Calistoga grapes, or change their names! They fought it hard. It finally got approved in 2009, and they got three years to comply.

Next door, Diamond Mountain had a fight over one word too, and the owners of a winery with that trademark won, so it's officially the Diamond Mountain District. And in Sonoma, a giant region called Northern Sonoma was created in 1985 largely because of the huge Gallo winery.

clips.title: The Gold Rush, and how it remade this whole region
clips.text:
Okay, let's talk about the event that made Sacramento, and, honestly, most of what you'll see today.

On the 24th of January 1848, James Marshall was building a sawmill for the pioneer John Sutter, up the American River, when he spotted something shiny in the water. Gold! Sutter tried to keep it secret, because he was worried a rush would wreck his plans for a farming empire. Quiz: who do you think spread the news anyway? Hint: you've already met him today. … Sam Brannan! And about 300,000 people poured into California. San Francisco went from about 200 people in 1846 to around 36,000 by 1852, and California became a state in 1850.

The Gold Rush echoes through this whole trip. West Sacramento was a rest stop for miners. Dixon started as a halfway stop for them. Alfred Tubbs made his fortune selling rope to the rush, then founded Chateau Montelena. Dr. Bale of the grist mill went off mining and died of a fever. And all those new people were thirsty, so vineyards spread across Napa and Sonoma in the 1850s.

But it was a catastrophe for Native Californians. Disease, hunger and violence made their populations collapse, and whole tribes were driven from their land, including the Patwin of this valley.

clips.title: The Delta: California's Holland
clips.text:
South of the freeway, out of sight, is one of the most important places in California: the Sacramento-San Joaquin River Delta. The Yolo Bypass floods drain into it, and so does about half of all the water that runs off California's land.

Here's how it formed. Around 560,000 years ago, water broke through the coastal mountains and carved the Carquinez Strait and San Francisco Bay. All the rivers had to squeeze out through that one narrow gap, which slowed them down. The tides pushed back up and slowed them even more, so the rivers dropped their mud and built a huge freshwater marsh full of channels and peat islands.

Then people drained it. Today there are about 57 reclaimed islands, ringed by 1,100 miles of levees. Quiz: when you drain peat soil, something weird happens to the land. What? … It sinks! The peat breaks down and blows away, so a lot of the Delta now sits below sea level, behind its levees. That's why it's nicknamed California's Holland. And giant pumps at the south end send Delta water to farms and to the cities of Southern California. So pretty much every California water fight ends up here.

clips.title: Tule fog: the valley's winter ghost
clips.text:
Here's a handy one if you ever drive this valley in winter. From November to March, after the first big rains, the Central Valley gets something called tule fog, named after the tule reeds that used to cover the wetlands.

On long, still winter nights, the damp ground cools fast, and the cold air near the ground gets trapped under warmer air above, until it turns into a thick, low blanket of fog. It can stretch over 400 miles, from Bakersfield to Red Bluff. Quiz: in 2005, tule fog was the number one cause of what in California? … Weather-related car accidents! So if you ever see this valley disappear into a white wall on a winter morning, slow way down. Today, in late October, we're just ahead of the season. Phew.

clips.title: Who does the work? Farm labour in the valleys
clips.text:
Every vineyard and orchard you pass depends on people who rarely show up in the wine brochures. Here's their story.

The first workers were Native Californians, often forced. The Patwin were made to work for free on ranches and in mines, and by 1870 only a few Native people remained in the Napa Valley, working as labourers and servants. In the late 1800s, Chinese and Japanese immigrants worked Vacaville's orchards. In World War Two there was even a camp of German prisoners of war near Windsor, put to work.

The biggest change was the Bracero Program, a deal between the U.S. and Mexico that started in Stockton in August 1942 to fill wartime labour shortages. Over 22 years, it offered millions of contracts to Mexican workers. Quiz: what minimum hourly wage were they promised? … Thirty cents an hour. The programme ended in 1964, and economists later found that ending it pushed farms toward machines.

Today, around a third of Napa County's people are Hispanic or Latino. And the tension between luxury and labour is very much alive: in 2026, Thomas Keller of the French Laundry opposed a plan for 120 apartments in Yountville for workers who'd been priced out of town.

clips.title: Why the Napa Valley isn't covered in houses
clips.text:
Have you noticed something about the Napa Valley floor? There are basically no housing developments or shopping malls between the towns. That's not luck. It's one of the most important land decisions in California history.

Neighbouring counties let big stretches of farmland turn into houses and shops. But in 1968, Napa's winemakers and civic leaders went the other way. Using a new state law that gave tax breaks for keeping land in farming, they created an agricultural preserve on the valley floor. Quiz: was Napa the first county in California to do this? … Yes! It was the first one in the state. It started at 23,000 acres and grew to over 30,000. Then in 1990, voters went further and froze county zoning changes for thirty years, unless two-thirds of voters agreed.

The fights never stop. Locals battled the Wine Train in the eighties. County rules even stop Castello di Amorosa from hosting weddings. And now the big fight is about whether the people who work here can afford to live here. The preserve kept the valley green. Who gets to live in it is the next argument.

clips.title: Cannabis: California's other crop
clips.text:
Wine isn't the only crop around here with a complicated legal history.

California has been at the front of cannabis politics for half a century. In 1972, it held the first ballot vote in the nation to legalise cannabis. Quiz: did it pass? … Nope! It failed. But in 1996, California became the first state to legalise medical cannabis, and in 2016, voters legalised recreational use, with 57 percent of the vote.

Legalisation turned out to be messy. Growers had to register and get permits, and more than half of the medical dispensaries closed. Legal businesses pay hefty taxes, while illegal growers keep going in remote rural areas. And it's all still illegal under federal law. So, a bit like the winemakers during Prohibition, today's cannabis farmers live in a weird legal twilight zone between what the state allows and what Washington forbids.

clips.title: The Russians in California
clips.text:
We've met Russians again and again today: a river, a mountain, a farm near Graton. So here's the whole story.

Russian traders pushed east across Siberia and the North Pacific, and in 1799 they set up a colony in Alaska. Their business was fur, especially sea otters. From 1803, American ship captains took Alaska Native hunters down the California coast to hunt otters, and between 1805 and 1812 alone they gathered over 22,000 pelts.

In 1812 the Russians built their own base, Fort Ross, on the Sonoma coast, in the land of the Kashaya Pomo. It was super diverse: Native Californians, Native Alaskans, Russians, Finns and Swedes, all together. They explored the river and planted a farm and vineyard near Graton. And the Spanish and Mexicans got so nervous that they built the mission at Sonoma partly to block them.

Quiz: in 1841 the Russians decided to sell Fort Ross. They offered it to General Vallejo, but the Mexican officials dithered. Who ended up buying it? … John Sutter! The same Sutter on whose land gold was discovered seven years later. Small world.

clips.title: The Grape King of California
clips.text:
Here's a wine story you won't hear in many tasting rooms.

California's first wine grape was the Mission grape, brought by the Spanish, and it ruled until about 1880. Then the Gold Rush created thirsty customers, and Agoston Haraszthy brought in cuttings from 165 of Europe's best vineyards. Charles Krug, a Prussian political dissident, learned winemaking from Haraszthy before starting his own winery in St. Helena.

And north of Santa Rosa, at the utopian colony of Fountain Grove, the vineyards were run by Nagasawa Kanaye. Quiz: what nickname do you think he earned? … The Grape King of California! He was one of the biggest winemakers in the state, and he threw lavish dinners for guests like John Muir, Thomas Edison and Henry Ford. And according to the history books, Fountain Grove's cellars kept flowing right through Prohibition. Wink.

It's a reminder that wine country's history is a lot more diverse than the fancy châteaux suggest: Spanish missionaries, a Hungarian adventurer, German and Italian immigrants, a Finnish sea captain, and a Grape King, all on land that was Pomo, Wappo, Miwok and Patwin for thousands of years.
